9489.e: The panda is found only in China. There it lives in mountain forests.

9490.q: How does the beaver spend most of the day?
9490.e: During the day the beaver usually retreats to its sheltered lodge and rests there. It becomes active mainly at dusk and at night.
9490.m: By day the beaver rests in its lodge.

9491.q: How does the common wall lizard often behave towards others of its kind?
a: Males defend their own small territory
All wall lizards always live in huge herds
They always hunt together in packs
9491.e: Males usually keep to a particular area and tolerate no rivals there. Females and young are often more tolerant of each other.
9491.m: Each male has its own small territory.

9492.q: Where does the Alpine newt spend the winter?
a: On land in a frost-free hiding place
In a warm country in the south
9492.e: After the spawning season the Alpine newt leaves the water. It spends the winter stiff and still under stones, wood or in holes in the ground where it does not freeze.
9492.m: Alpine newts spend the winter on land.

9494.q: How often does a young garden cross spider moult before it is adult?
a: Only once in its whole life
9494.e: The spider’s hard skin does not grow with it. That is why a young garden cross spider moults several times until it is fully grown.
9494.m: It moults several times in its life.

9495.q: How much does a red fox usually weigh?
9495.e: An adult red fox usually weighs between five and seven kilograms. That is roughly twice as much as a large house cat.
9495.m: A fox weighs about five to seven kilos.

9496.q: How many teats does a goat’s udder usually have?
9496.e: Unlike a cow, a goat usually has only two teats on its udder. The kid drinks its milk from them.
9496.m: A goat’s udder has two teats.

9497.q: What are the little heaps of soil that earthworms leave on the surface called?
9497.e: These are small heaps of digested soil that the worm leaves behind. You often find them on meadows in the morning.

a: Yes, it can swim but usually avoids water
9498.e: Stone martens can swim well when needed but prefer dry ground. They usually only cross water when they have to.
9498.m: Stone martens swim only when they must.

9499.q: Who is the head of the Roman Catholic Church?
9499.e: The Pope lives in the Vatican in Rome and is the most important representative of the Catholic Church worldwide. He is elected by the cardinals.
9499.m: The Pope leads the Catholic Church.

9500.q: What is especially striking about adult male baboons?
9500.e: The males’ canine teeth can grow very long. They are used for defence and for threatening.

9501.q: What is the best way to recognise an earwig?
a: By the pincers at the end of its body
By the snail shell on its back
9501.e: The pincers at the end of the abdomen are typical of the earwig. No other native insect looks like this.
9501.m: The pincers at the end of the body give the earwig away.

9502.q: In which habitat are tigers often found?
9502.e: Tigers live in dense forests, jungles and grasslands in Asia. There they find enough cover and prey.

9503.q: Some river power stations have a fish ladder made of many small pools. What is it for?
a: Fish can use it to get past weirs
Fish spend the winter in it
It keeps birds of prey away
9503.e: A fish ladder consists of small steps with pools. This lets fish swim upstream past weirs and dams.
9503.m: Fish ladders help fish over obstacles.

9504.q: Where does a female budgie lay her eggs?
a: In the grass on the ground
In an open nest on a branch
In a hole in the sand
9504.e: Female budgies lay their eggs in small holes, often in hollow trees. As pets they use a nest box.
9504.m: Budgies lay eggs in tree holes.

9506.q: Roughly how long is an okapi’s tongue?
9506.e: The tongue is very long and flexible. The okapi can even clean its eyes and ears with it.
9506.m: Okapis have an extremely long tongue.

9507.q: How many humps does a dromedary have?
9507.e: The dromedary is also called the one-humped camel. Its single hump sits on its back.
9507.m: The dromedary is the domestic camel with one hump.

9508.q: What does a starfish usually do all day?
a: It crawls slowly over the seabed
It flies from place to place
It digs tunnels like a mole
9508.e: Starfish mostly spend their time crawling slowly over the seabed. While doing so they look for food.
9508.m: Starfish crawl around on the bottom.

9509.q: What is the flight called in which the peregrine falcon plunges steeply onto its prey with its wings folded in?
9509.e: In a stoop the falcon folds its wings close to its body and dives down like an arrow. This is how it reaches its top speeds.
9509.m: The stoop makes the falcon incredibly fast.

9510.q: What does an adult green sea turtle like to eat most?
9510.e: Adult green sea turtles feed mainly on seagrass and algae. The young, on the other hand, still eat more small animals.

9511.q: Which habitats does the beaver prefer in Switzerland?
a: Banks of rivers, streams and lakes with trees and shrubs
9511.e: The beaver needs waters with wooded banks where plenty of willows and poplars grow. It finds such habitats on many rivers and lakes in the Swiss lowlands.
9511.m: Beavers need waters with trees and shrubs.

9512.q: What does a fox hear especially well with?
9512.e: The fox’s large, pointed ears can hear even quiet sounds such as a mouse rustling. This helps it a lot when hunting.

9514.q: What is special about llamas’ red blood cells?
a: They are as huge as peas
9514.e: Unlike in most mammals, they are oval. This helps llamas at high altitude with little oxygen.
9514.m: Llamas have oval red blood cells.

9515.q: What does an adult kestrel’s tail typically look like?
a: Long, with a broad black band at the end
Round like a peacock’s with many eyespots
9515.e: The kestrel’s tail is fairly long and ends in a clearly visible black band. In the male the tail is also blue-grey.
9515.m: A black band decorates the tail.

9516.q: How heavy can an adult African buffalo bull get?
9516.e: Large bulls often weigh more than half a tonne. This makes them very powerful animals, but much lighter than elephants.
9516.m: Bulls weigh up to about 900 kilograms.

9517.q: Roughly how big is an adult African wild dog?
a: About as big as a large German shepherd
9517.e: Its shoulder height is about 60 to 75 centimetres. It usually weighs 18 to 36 kilograms.
9517.m: About as big as a German shepherd.

9519.q: What colour are the legs and feet of an adult peregrine falcon usually?
9519.e: The legs and feet of adult peregrine falcons are a striking yellow. This makes them easy to tell apart from some other birds of prey.
9519.m: Yellow feet are typical of the peregrine falcon.

9520.q: What do geese like to eat most?
9520.e: Geese are mainly plant eaters. They pluck grass and other green plants with their beaks.

9523.q: What happens to a slow worm’s tail after it has shed it?
a: It only grows back as a short stump
It grows back longer than before
The old tail grows back on
A leg grows in its place
9523.e: The shed tail only grows back partly. A short, blunt stump remains.
9523.m: The tail only grows back short.

9524.q: Which statement about the snow leopard’s fur is correct?
a: It is very thick and long, especially on the belly
It has hair only on the head
9524.e: On the belly the fur can be several centimetres long. This protects against the cold.
9524.m: Thick fur protects against the cold.

9525.q: Why can global warming become a problem for lake trout?
a: Warm water makes the fish too heavy
Warm water drives away all insects
9525.e: When lakes and streams warm up, less oxygen dissolves in the water. Cold-water fish like the lake trout then come under stress.

9526.q: How does the great tit usually get about?
9526.e: The great tit flies skilfully from branch to branch and also hops about among the twigs. It is very agile and nimble.
9526.m: Great tits fly nimbly from branch to branch.

9527.q: Which sounds do African wild dogs use to communicate, among others?
9527.e: Wild dogs twitter and squeak to communicate. They also use body language.
9527.m: Wild dogs communicate with squeaks and calls.

9528.q: What are a plant’s leaves especially important for?
a: They hold the plant in the ground
9528.e: In the leaves the plant makes its own food with the help of sunlight, water and air. This happens mainly in the green leaves.

9530.q: How many little feet can a starfish have in total?
9530.e: A starfish has several hundred tiny feet on its underside. They help it move and hold on.
9530.m: Many hundreds of little feet on the body.

9531.q: How are baby guinea pigs born?
a: Already able to see and with fur
9531.e: Unlike many other rodents, baby guinea pigs are born well developed. Shortly after birth they can already see, walk and even try a little food.
9531.m: Baby guinea pigs are born ready to go.

a: A slip on which you tick Yes or No
A letter from the Federal Council
9532.e: On the ballot paper you tick what you think about a question. This way you can help decide in a vote.

9533.q: What is an ischial callosity in baboons?
a: A hardened, hairless patch of skin on the bottom
A fat pad on the back
A flap of skin on the neck
9533.e: Baboons have hard, furless sitting pads. They act as cushions when sitting on hard ground.

9535.q: What does a golden eagle’s call usually sound like?
a: High and rather quiet for its size
Extremely loud like a lion’s roar
It makes no sounds at all
9535.e: Although the golden eagle is a very large bird, its calls are rather high and fairly quiet. You hear it much less often than you see it.
9535.m: Its calls are high but rather quiet.

9536.q: What hatches first from common frog eggs?
9536.e: Tadpoles hatch from the eggs first; they live in the water and breathe with gills. Only later do they change into small frogs.

9537.q: How do buffalo cows react when a calf is in danger?
a: They often defend it with their horns
They leave it behind at once
They hide it in a cave
They carry it on their backs
9537.e: Cows protect their calves fiercely. Sometimes other members of the herd help too.

9538.q: Roughly how long is the pregnancy of ring-tailed lemurs?
a: Around four and a half months
9538.e: The baby is born after about 135 days. That is around four and a half months.

9539.q: Roughly how long does the bearded vulture incubate its eggs before the chick hatches?
9539.e: The parents sit on the eggs for about 53 to 58 days. Only then does the chick hatch.

9540.q: What does it mean that goldfish are shoaling fish?
a: They feel better in the company of other goldfish
9540.e: By nature goldfish like living together with other fish. That is why they should not be kept alone.

9541.q: Why can gibbons swing through the trees so fast?
a: Long arms, a light body and flexible wrists
They have suction pads on their feet
9541.e: Long arms, low weight and flexible wrists work together. This lets them swing far and smoothly.
9541.m: Their build makes gibbons swinging experts.

9542.q: How does a penguin catch its prey?
a: It dives and catches it with its beak
It lies in wait on land
9542.e: Penguins are very skilful divers. They hunt fish and krill right in the water with their pointed beaks.

9543.q: In which country do bonobos live in the wild?
9543.e: Bonobos live only in the rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo in Africa. Nowhere else in the world are they found in the wild.
9543.m: Wild bonobos live only in the Congo.

9544.q: Roughly how far can a bearded vulture fly in a day while looking for food?
9544.e: Thanks to its large wings, a bearded vulture can glide huge distances over the mountains. In this way it searches a very large area for bones and carrion.
9544.m: Huge distances in search of food.

9545.q: Roughly how many different kinds of earthworm are there in the whole world?
9545.e: There are thousands of different earthworm species worldwide. They differ in size, colour and habitat.
9545.m: There are very many earthworm species.

9546.q: What does the term bottom-dwelling fish mean?
a: A fish that often stays on the bottom of the water
A fish that lives only at the surface
A fish that lives only in the sea
A fish that lives on land
9546.e: The wels catfish usually stays near the bottom. There it finds hiding places and prey.
9546.m: Bottom-dwelling fish live near the bottom of the water.

9547.q: Complete the German saying: “As proud as a …”
9547.e: The German saying “as proud as a cockerel” describes people who behave very confidently and stand tall. It comes from the proud strut of the cockerel in the farmyard. In English people say “as proud as a peacock”.
9547.m: “As proud as a cockerel” is a German saying.

9548.q: What role do females play in a bonobo group?
a: They have a strong, leading position
They must always leave the food to the males
They live alone and avoid the group
9548.e: Among bonobos, females have a strong position. Because they stick together, they can hold their own well against the males.
9548.m: Among bonobos, females have a lot of influence.

9549.q: Roughly how wide can a common raven’s wingspan be?
9549.e: The common raven has very long wings that give it a wingspan of up to 1.3 metres. This makes it an excellent flier.
9549.m: The common raven has a wingspan of up to about 1.3 metres.

9550.q: What do newly hatched lake trout live on at first?
9550.e: The larvae still carry a store of nutrients on their bellies. They live on it until they hunt food themselves.
9550.m: The yolk sac is their first packed lunch.

9551.q: Why do blue whales often travel long distances through the oceans?
a: To move between feeding grounds and breeding areas
9551.e: Blue whales travel between areas with lots of krill and warmer waters for their young. These journeys can be thousands of kilometres long.

a: A carp with almost no scales
A carp with many small scales
A carp with a few large scales
A carp with scales only on its belly
9552.e: The leather carp is a bred variety that has almost no scales. Its skin therefore feels as smooth as leather.
9552.m: Leather carp have almost no scales.

9554.q: Apart from sweet things, what else does a wasp like to eat?
9554.e: Adult wasps do not only eat sweet things. They also hunt small insects, some of which they feed to their larvae.

9555.q: What role does the cockerel often take when the group finds food?
a: He often lets the hens eat first
He always eats everything first on his own
9555.e: A cockerel often calls the hens to the food and frequently lets them go first. This shows his caring behaviour towards the group.
9555.m: The cockerel often lets the hens eat first.

9556.q: What does the black rhino mainly eat?
9556.e: With its pointed lip, the black rhino can pluck leaves from bushes and twigs. The white rhino, on the other hand, mainly eats grass.

9557.q: Where does the great crested newt lay its eggs?
9557.e: The female wraps each egg separately in the leaf of a water plant. The larvae grow up in the water.
9557.m: Great crested newts lay their eggs in water.

9558.q: Roughly how long do tiger cubs stay with their mother?
9558.e: Tiger cubs stay with their mother for about two years. During this time they learn to hunt.
9558.m: Tiger cubs stay with their mother for two years.

9559.e: Blue whales swim in almost all the large seas on Earth. They often travel very long distances.
9559.m: Blue whales live in the oceans.

9560.q: What is a female guinea pig called?
9560.e: Female guinea pigs are called sows. The name has nothing to do with pigs on the farm.
9560.m: A female guinea pig is called a sow.

9561.q: When was the beaver reintroduced to Switzerland after it had died out?
9561.e: After the beaver had been wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century, reintroduction began in the 20th century. Today there are many beaver territories in the country again.

9562.q: Why do orangutans only rarely have babies?
a: The gaps between births are very long
They only mate every hundred years
The females usually cannot have babies
9562.e: There are often six to eight years between two births. This is the longest gap between births of any land mammal.
9562.m: Orangutans have long gaps between births.

9563.q: Which animals are among the enemies of the slow worm?
a: Hedgehogs, birds of prey and foxes
9563.e: Cats, martens and snakes such as the smooth snake also eat them. That is why hiding places are important.

9564.q: What are stinging cells in a jellyfish?
a: Tiny cells with poison that can sting
9564.e: Stinging cells contain fine poison threads. If prey touches the tentacles, the threads shoot out and paralyse it.
9564.m: Stinging cells contain poison for stinging.

9565.q: What is the smallest number of budgies that should be kept together?
9565.e: Because budgies are sociable flock birds, at least two should always be kept together. That way they do not feel lonely.
9565.m: Budgies are kept at least in pairs.

9566.q: How do adult great crested grebes most often get about?
9566.e: Great crested grebes are perfectly adapted to life in the water and spend most of their lives swimming and diving. They hardly move on land.
9566.m: Swimming and diving shape its life.

9567.q: What does a roe deer usually do first, just before it starts to eat?
a: It looks and listens carefully around it
9567.e: Roe deer are cautious animals. Before they eat, they first look and listen around them to spot danger.
9567.m: Roe deer check their surroundings before eating.

9568.q: What is blubber in a dolphin?
a: A thick layer of fat under the skin
9568.e: Blubber is the name for the thick layer of fat under a dolphin’s skin. It protects against cold and stores energy.
9568.m: Blubber is the layer of fat under the skin.

9569.q: How good is a wild boar’s nose?
a: Very good, it has an excellent sense of smell
9569.e: Wild boar have a very fine nose. With it they find food, even when it is hidden deep in the ground.
9569.m: The wild boar’s nose is top class.

9572.q: How do adult orangutans usually live?
9572.e: Adult orangutans usually go about alone. Only mothers with young stay together.

9573.q: How can you tell a stone marten from a pine marten?
a: By the white, forked throat patch
By the length of the tail
By the fur colour on the back
By the size of the ears
9573.e: The stone marten has a white throat patch that is usually split in two, while the pine marten has a yellowish, rounded patch. This feature helps tell them apart reliably.
9573.m: A white forked patch shows a stone marten.

9574.q: Which endangered animal lives in the wild only in China and eats almost nothing but bamboo?
9574.e: The giant panda lives in the mountain forests of China and feeds almost entirely on bamboo. Thanks to conservation programmes, its numbers have recently recovered slightly.
9574.m: Pandas live in the wild only in China.

9575.q: What do dolphins like to eat most?
9575.e: Dolphins are hunters and eat fish and squid. They grab the slippery prey with their pointed teeth.

9576.q: What protects your brain from knocks?
9576.e: The skull is a hard bone that surrounds your brain like a helmet. That way it is well protected.
9576.m: The skull is the brain's helmet.

9577.q: How do young perch often live?
9577.e: Young perch often swim in groups. In a group they are better protected from enemies.

9578.q: Roughly how old can a duck get in the wild?
9578.e: Wild ducks such as the mallard can live for several years in the wild. Some even reach over ten years.
9578.m: Ducks often live for several years.

9579.q: What does a young lamb’s wool feel like?
a: Smooth and short like a horse’s
9579.e: Young lambs often have especially soft and sometimes curly fleece. This first coat of wool is called lambswool.

9580.q: What do fossils show about tapirs?
a: Tapir-like animals have existed for millions of years
Tapirs have only existed for 100 years
Tapirs used to live only in the sea
9580.e: Tapir-like animals have existed for around 50 million years. They have changed only a little since then.
9580.m: Tapirs are an ancient group of animals.

9581.q: Who forecasts on television whether it will rain or be sunny tomorrow?
9581.e: Meteorologists collect weather data and use it to make forecasts. That is how we find out what the weather will be like tomorrow.

9582.q: Which parts of plants does the beaver especially prefer in winter?
a: Bark and twigs of willows and poplars
9582.e: In winter, when soft plants are missing, the beaver feeds mainly on bark and twigs, especially from willows and poplars. It gathers these supplies in autumn.
9582.m: In winter the beaver eats bark.

9583.q: In which sea is the European perch found in slightly salty water?
9583.e: The European perch can cope with slightly salty brackish water and lives, for example, in the Baltic Sea. But fresh water is its main habitat.
9583.m: The perch can live in the brackish Baltic Sea.

9584.q: Which large green insect with very long antennae jumps through Swiss meadows in summer?
9584.e: The great green bush-cricket is one of the largest grasshopper-like insects in Switzerland. You can recognise it by its very long antennae.
9584.m: The great green bush-cricket has very long antennae.

9586.q: Roughly how old can a great spotted woodpecker get in the wild?
9586.e: If it finds enough food and meets no enemies, a great spotted woodpecker can live for several years. Ten years is already quite a lot.
9586.m: It can live up to ten years.

9587.q: How good is the peregrine falcon’s eyesight compared with a human’s?
a: Much better, it spots prey from a great distance
It sees only outlines without colours
9587.e: Peregrine falcons have very sharp eyes and can spot prey from a long way off. This sharp eyesight is vital for successful hunting.
9587.m: Sharp eyes spot prey from afar.

9588.q: What does an earthworm do when its tunnel suddenly fills with water?
a: It crawls up to the surface
It just stays where it is
9588.e: When the tunnels are full of water, the worm gets too little air. So it prefers to come up until it is drier again.

9590.q: How fast can a bison run over short distances?
9590.e: Despite their weight, bison are very fast. They can cover short distances at about 50 km/h and more.
9590.m: Bison are very fast despite their bulk.

9591.q: What does an adult perch eat?
a: Insect larvae, crayfish and small fish
Only plant remains from the bank
9591.e: Large perch are predatory fish. They hunt small fish, crustaceans and insect larvae.
9591.m: The perch is a predatory fish.

9592.q: How does the adder have its young?
a: The young hatch from egg membranes right at birth
9592.e: The adder gives birth to live young. The eggs develop inside the mother’s body, and the young are born in thin egg membranes, which they leave at once.
9592.m: Adders give birth to live young.

9593.q: What is the planet Saturn especially known for?
a: Its striking ring system of ice and rock
Its solid surface you can walk on
9593.e: Saturn has wide, clearly visible rings made of countless small pieces of ice and rock. They make it especially easy to recognise through a telescope.
9593.m: Saturn has a large, clearly visible ring system.

9594.q: What does the huge whale shark like to eat most?
a: Tiny living things such as plankton
9594.e: The whale shark swims through the water with its mouth open and filters out tiny creatures. Despite its size it is completely harmless.
9594.m: Whale sharks filter plankton out of the water.

9596.q: Why do African buffalo like to wallow in mud?
a: To cool down and protect themselves from insects
9596.e: The layer of mud cools them and keeps flies and other pests away. When it dries, it also protects the skin.
9596.m: Mud cools and protects against insects.

9597.q: Which stages of development does a dung beetle go through, in the right order?
9597.e: This is called complete metamorphosis. The larva looks completely different from the finished beetle.

9598.q: What is the special flying technique called in which the kestrel practically stands still in the air?
9598.e: When hovering, the kestrel beats its wings fast to stay at one point in the air. That way it can search the ground closely for prey.
9598.m: Hovering lets the kestrel stand still in the air.

9599.q: What does a butterfly need to be able to fly well?
9599.e: Butterflies are cold-blooded, so their bodies need warmth from outside. Only when the sun warms up their flight muscles can they fly properly.
9599.m: Warmth from the sun helps with flying.

9600.q: What do magpies often line the inside of their nests with?
a: With clay, soil and soft material
9600.e: Inside the nest, magpies form a layer of clay or soil, which they pad with soft material such as roots or hair. This makes a cosy hollow for the eggs.
9600.m: Magpie nests have a soft inner layer.

a: A large community of living things with a typical climate, plants and animals
A single tree in a forest
9601.e: Biomes are large habitats such as tundra, steppe or rainforest, shaped by a characteristic climate and typical plants and animals. They occur in similar forms on different continents.
9601.m: Biomes are large habitats typical of a climate.

a: Steady winds near the equator that blow from high to low air pressure
Winds that only occur in the Alps
Winds that only blow in winter
9602.e: Trade winds are very regular winds that blow near the equator. In the past they were important for sailing ships.
9602.m: Trade winds blow regularly towards the equator.

9603.q: How does the Alpine newt move on land?
9603.e: On land the Alpine newt moves rather slowly and crawls on its four short legs. In the water, on the other hand, it is a skilful swimmer.
9603.m: On land the Alpine newt crawls slowly.

9605.q: How does the prey of a single wolf differ from that of a whole pack?
a: A pack can also kill large animals such as deer
A single wolf always hunts bigger animals
9605.e: On its own, a wolf usually only manages to kill smaller prey, while a whole pack together can overpower large hoofed animals too. Working together makes the pack especially successful.
9605.m: In a pack, big hunts succeed too.

9608.q: What is the octopus’s ability to blend in perfectly with its surroundings called?
9608.e: Camouflage is when an animal changes so that it can hardly be seen. The octopus is a master of camouflage.

9609.q: Which animal builds dams and lodges in rivers with branches?
9609.e: The beaver dams a river with branches and twigs to create a calm pond. In it, it builds its beaver lodge.
9609.m: The beaver is a skilful builder.

9610.q: Which animal is a beetle, like the ladybird?
9610.e: Ladybirds and cockchafers both belong to the beetles. Beetles have hard wing cases that protect their delicate flying wings.

9611.q: Roughly how many fins does a trout have on its whole body?
a: Several, for example on the back, belly and tail
Only two fins on the head
9611.e: A trout has several different fins spread over its whole body. These include, for example, the dorsal fin, the pelvic fins and the tail fin.
9611.m: Trout have several fins on their body.

9612.q: What does the word “rhinoceros” actually mean?
9612.e: The name comes from Greek and means “nose horn”, because the rhinoceros has a horn on its nose. That is how the animal got its name.

9613.q: What does a horse absolutely need in its stable?
a: Lots of space and access to the outdoors
A tiny cage with no window
9613.e: Horses need lots of space to move and should be able to go outside as often as possible. A stable that is too cramped makes them unhappy.
9613.m: Horses need lots of space and time outdoors.

9614.q: At what time of year are sand lizards most active in Switzerland?
a: From spring to autumn, in warm weather
Only in the depths of winter
All year round in sub-zero temperatures
9614.e: As soon as it gets warmer in spring, the animals leave their winter quarters. In autumn, as temperatures fall, they withdraw again.
9614.m: Active from spring to autumn when it is warm.

9615.q: What does an Alpine ibex like to eat most in summer?
9615.e: In summer, ibex feed mainly on juicy Alpine herbs, grasses and flowers on the mountain meadows. They eat only plants.
9615.m: Ibex eat Alpine herbs and grasses.

9616.q: What is special about the tiger among the cats?
a: It is the largest cat species in the world
It is the smallest cat species in the world
It is the only cat that lays eggs
It is the only cat without claws
9616.e: The tiger is the largest living cat species. The Siberian tiger in particular can weigh over 250 kilograms.
9616.m: The tiger is the largest cat.

9617.q: What does a sparrow like to eat most of all?
9617.e: Sparrows like to peck small seeds and grains from the ground. In summer they also like to eat insects.

9618.q: In the picture a trout is hiding. Where does it like to stay?
a: Under stones, roots and overhanging banks
On dry land on the bank
In the middle of a bare concrete slab
9618.e: Such hiding places protect it from enemies and from the strong current. It also lies in wait for prey from there.
9618.m: It hides under stones and roots.

9619.q: Roughly how many years can a Bactrian camel live?
9619.e: In human care they can reach an age of about 40 to 50 years. That is long for mammals of this size.

9620.q: What happens when chimpanzees tickle and play with each other?
a: They make a panting laugh sound
9620.e: When chimpanzees play and are tickled, they make a sound that is a bit like laughing. This shows that they are having fun.
9620.m: Chimpanzees can laugh when they play.

9621.q: How does a goat usually carry its tail compared with a sheep?
a: Always dragging flat on the ground
It has no tail at all
9621.e: Goats usually hold their short tail up, while sheep often let it hang down. This is a small difference between the two species.

9622.q: What does the red kite use to steer its flight especially skilfully?
9622.e: The deeply forked tail can be turned and shifted like a rudder. This lets the red kite fly very elegantly and nimbly.
9622.m: The tail steers the red kite’s flight.

9623.q: What does a magnifying glass do to the sun's rays?
a: It focuses them on one point
It turns them into heat without light
9623.e: A magnifying glass is curved and bends the light rays so that they meet at one point. It can get so hot there that paper starts to burn.
9623.m: A magnifying glass focuses light on one point.

9624.q: What does “cold-blooded” mean for an animal like the lizard?
a: Its body temperature adjusts to its surroundings
9624.e: Cold-blooded animals such as reptiles cannot control their body temperature themselves. That is why they often sunbathe to warm up.

9625.q: What colour is a polar bear’s fur usually?
9625.e: The polar bear’s fur is white to slightly yellowish. That way it is well camouflaged in the snow.
9625.m: The fur is white to yellowish.

9626.q: What do wasps often hunt as food for their larvae?
9626.e: Wasps catch small insects such as flies or caterpillars. They feed these to their hungry larvae.
9626.m: Wasps hunt flies for their larvae.

9627.q: In which regions do moose mainly live?
9627.e: Moose need cool forests with lakes and swamps. They are found in Scandinavia, Russia and North America.
9627.m: Moose live in cool northern forests.

9628.q: What does a carrion crow mainly eat?
a: almost anything, for example insects, carrion, seeds and eggs
9628.e: Carrion crows eat almost anything and feed on insects, carrion, grains, fruit and sometimes also eggs or chicks of other species. This variety helps them survive.

9629.q: What do rhinos do during the day when it is very hot?
a: They rest in the shade or in mud
They dig themselves into the ground
9629.e: In great heat, rhinos look for a shady spot or lie down in a cool mud puddle. That way they protect themselves from the sun.
9629.m: In the heat, rhinos rest in the shade.

9630.q: What do male hippos use to defend themselves against rivals?
9630.e: Male hippos have very long, sharp canine teeth. They use them to fight each other for their territory.

9631.q: How do its fins help the goldfish?
9631.e: With its fins the goldfish can swim forwards, brake and change direction. Different breeds have fins of different lengths.
9631.m: Fins help with swimming and steering.

9632.q: How big is the mute swan compared with a duck?
9632.e: The mute swan is one of the largest waterbirds and is clearly bigger than an ordinary duck. You can recognise it from far away.
9632.m: Mute swans are much bigger than ducks.

9633.q: In many falcon species, including the kestrel, what is typical of the size of males and females?
a: The female is usually a little bigger than the male
The male is always much bigger
Both are always exactly the same size
9633.e: In many birds of prey, including the kestrel, the females are a little bigger and heavier than the males. This is called reversed size difference.
9633.m: Females are usually bigger than males.

9634.q: What are the little lumps of pollen on a bumblebee’s legs called?
9634.e: These lumps on the hind legs are called pollen loads. You can see them well when the bumblebee flies from flower to flower.
9634.m: Pollen lumps are called pollen loads.

9635.q: How long can a dromedary manage without water in the desert?
a: Several days, even longer in cool weather
Not at all, it must drink every day
9635.e: Dromedaries can cope with a large loss of water and then drink a great deal at once. How long it works depends on heat and food.

9636.q: How can you vote without going to the ballot box in person?
a: With a show of hands in the classroom
9636.e: Many people in Switzerland vote by post. They send in their ballot paper by mail.

9637.q: How do leafcutter ants carry their pieces of leaf?
a: In their mouths like a sponge
On their backs like a hump
9637.e: The ants hold the piece of leaf high above their heads with their jaws. Long lines of them look like little green flags.
9637.m: Pieces of leaf are carried above the head.

9638.q: What do adult whitefish mainly feed on?
9638.e: Whitefish mainly eat zooplankton, that is small animals floating in the water. These include, for example, water fleas.

9639.q: Roughly how long does it take for a lamb to be born (pregnancy)?
9639.e: A mother sheep carries her lamb in her belly for about five months before it is born. After that the lamb can soon walk by itself.
9639.m: A lamb grows for about five months.

9640.q: What colour is the red panda’s fur mainly?
a: Black and white like the giant panda
9640.e: The red panda looks different from its big namesake. Its fur is mainly reddish brown.
9640.m: The red panda is reddish brown.

9641.q: Which animal is a close relative of the Alpine newt?
9641.e: The Alpine newt and the fire salamander belong to the same family, the true salamanders. Frogs and toads are more distant relatives, and the slow worm is a lizard.
9641.m: The Alpine newt and the fire salamander are closely related.

9642.q: How does a barn swallow usually fly when hunting insects?
a: Low over meadows, water or fields
Always extremely high above the clouds
Not at all, it hunts on the ground
9642.e: When hunting, the barn swallow usually flies low over meadows, water or fields, where lots of insects are about. There it catches the insects in fast flight.
9642.m: It flies low over meadows when hunting.

9643.q: Which kind of baboon also lives in Asia?
a: The hamadryas baboon, on the Arabian Peninsula
9643.e: The hamadryas baboon lives in north-east Africa and in the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula. There it is found, for example, in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
9643.m: Hamadryas baboons also live in Arabia.

9644.q: Apart from roe deer, which prey does the lynx sometimes eat?
9644.e: Besides roe deer, the lynx also hunts smaller animals such as hares or birds. Sometimes it also catches young foxes.
9644.m: The lynx eats a varied diet of meat.

9645.q: What does a grasshopper most often do first when in danger?
a: It jumps away in a flash
It stands completely still and falls asleep
It immediately digs a deep hole
9645.e: Thanks to its strong hind legs, it can make a big escape jump at once. That way it escapes many enemies.
9645.m: In a flash, it is gone.

9646.q: Which measure helps to protect bonobos?
a: Catching them for the animal trade
9646.e: Protected areas preserve the habitat, and hunting bans help the animals directly. Educating local people is also important.

9647.q: What do hamsters like to do with branches and wood?
9647.e: Hamsters like gnawing on branches. This helps them keep their ever-growing teeth short.

9648.q: What is typical of the slow worm’s head?
a: It joins the body with almost no neck
It is broad like a viper’s
9648.e: Head and body form almost one line. This helps it wriggle through thick grass.
9648.m: The head joins the body without a neck.

9649.q: Why do common swifts often run into trouble when buildings are renovated?
a: their nesting sites in wall cracks are often sealed up
the houses are painted too brightly for them
it gets too noisy for them in town
the new roofs are too heavy for them
9649.e: During renovations, cracks and niches in house walls are often sealed. As a result, swifts lose their traditional nesting sites.
9649.m: Renovations often destroy swift nesting sites.

9651.q: What does a dog often do before lying down to sleep?
a: It turns round in a circle several times
It washes itself with its tongue
It digs a deep hole in the house
9651.e: Many dogs turn round in a circle several times before they lie down. This behaviour probably comes from their wild ancestors, who made themselves a comfortable bed this way.
9651.m: Before sleeping, a dog often turns round.

9652.q: Roughly how much does a least weasel weigh?
9652.e: The weight depends greatly on sex and season. Males are clearly heavier than females.

9653.q: Why were geese especially important in a famous old story from Rome?
a: Their loud honking warned people of enemies at night
They guarded a treasure in the forest
9653.e: According to legend, geese raised the alarm with their loud honking at night when enemies were secretly approaching. In this way they are said to have saved the city of Rome.
9653.m: Geese warned of enemies with their honking.

9654.q: Why are sheep important for farming families in the Swiss mountains?
a: They provide wool, meat and sometimes milk
They guard the house like a dog
9654.e: Sheep are important for mountain farming families because they provide wool, meat and sometimes milk. They also look after the steep Alpine pastures by grazing them.
9654.m: Sheep provide wool, meat and milk.

9655.q: What colour is the flesh of wild salmon usually?
9655.e: The flesh gets its colour from pigments in the food, for example from tiny crustaceans. That is why it is pink to orange.
9655.m: Salmon flesh is pink because of its food.

9656.q: What is special about the stag beetle in Europe?
a: It is one of the largest beetles
It is the only beetle that swims
It is the only poisonous beetle
9656.e: Large males, including their antlers, grow up to about 8 centimetres long. This makes the stag beetle one of the largest beetles in Europe.
9656.m: The stag beetle is one of Europe’s largest beetles.

9658.q: Trout have a small extra fin without bony rays on their back, just before the tail fin. What is it called?
9658.e: Fish of the salmon family such as the brown trout have a small adipose fin in addition to the dorsal fin. It has no bony rays.
9658.m: Salmon-family fish have a small adipose fin.

9659.q: How can you recognise an orca in the water from far away?
a: By a horn on its nose
9659.e: The tall dorsal fin sticks far out of the water. That is how you recognise the orca at once.
9659.m: Orcas have a tall dorsal fin.

9660.q: What do two little giraffe calves sometimes do to play?
a: They run and play with each other in the group
They swim together in the sea
9660.e: Young giraffes like to play with each other and already practise fighting with their necks. This way they learn important skills for later.
9660.m: Young giraffes play and practise together.

9661.q: What appears first when a tadpole hatches from a frog’s egg?
a: A small body with a tail and outer gills
9661.e: The newly hatched tadpole has a tail for swimming and outer gills for breathing. Only later do legs and lungs develop.
9661.m: The tadpole first has a tail and gills, then it grows legs.

9663.q: Why is the wels catfish an introduced species in some regions?
a: People released it into new waters
9663.e: In some countries people put wels catfish into lakes and rivers. There it can affect the native fish.
9663.m: People have spread wels catfish widely.

9665.q: Where does a wild rabbit like to live best?
9665.e: Wild rabbits dig underground holes and tunnels where they hide and sleep. There they are protected from enemies.

9666.q: Roughly how soon can a newborn reindeer calf walk?
a: After just a few hours, with the herd
Not at all, it is carried
9666.e: Reindeer calves are well developed at birth and stand up quickly. After a short time they can follow the herd.

a: Yes, it flies fast and for a long time
No, it cannot fly at all
It can only hop a few centimetres high
9667.e: Although it swims on the water, the mallard can also fly very well. It covers long distances when doing so.

9668.q: Which animal group does the starfish belong to?
9668.e: Starfish belong to the group of echinoderms, which means “spiny skins”. These animals all have a spiny body.

9669.q: How does the sand lizard have its young?
a: It gives birth to live young
It feeds its young with milk
9669.e: The sand lizard lays its eggs in warm, loose soil. There the sun warms them until the young hatch.

9670.q: Which family does the llama belong to?
9670.e: Llamas belong to the camel family. But they are at home in South America and have no hump.
9670.m: Llamas are camels without a hump.

9671.q: Apart from crawling, what can starfish do with their little feet?
a: Swim fast as if with fins
9671.e: The little feet do not only help the starfish crawl. It can also hold on with them and pull mussels open.
9671.m: Little feet also help it hold on.

9672.q: Why do wild boar often have mud on their bodies?
a: Because they like wallowing in mud
Because they live in the river
Because they want to hide in it
9672.e: Wild boar regularly bathe in the mud of their wallow. This is good for their skin and cools them down.
9672.m: Mud on the body comes from the wallow.

9673.q: What were water frogs such as the edible frog also used for in some regions in the past?
a: As food, their hind legs were eaten
As guards in front of houses
9673.e: In some regions of Europe, the hind legs of water frogs were eaten as a delicacy, known as frogs’ legs. This is probably also where the species name esculentus, meaning edible, comes from.
9673.m: Frogs’ legs used to be eaten.

9674.q: Roughly how fast can a penguin swim in the water?
9674.e: Penguins are very fast swimmers. Some species reach speeds of up to 25 kilometres per hour in the water.

9675.q: Why is it important for guinea pigs to get things to gnaw such as branches?
a: So that their teeth do not get too long
So that they can build trees
So that they learn to swim
So that they can smell better
9675.e: As well as hay, branches and twigs help wear down their ever-growing teeth. That way the teeth stay a healthy length.

9676.q: How can you tell that a goose feels comfortable?
9676.e: A relaxed goose takes time to arrange its feathers carefully with its beak. This shows that it feels safe and well.

9677.q: Why are brown bears protected in many European countries?
a: Because their numbers fell sharply in the past and they need protection
Because they are meant to be kept as pets
Because otherwise there would quickly be too many
9677.e: In the past, brown bears were hunted heavily in many parts of Europe, so their numbers fell sharply. That is why they are protected in many countries today, so that their population can recover.
9677.m: Brown bears are strictly protected today.

9678.q: Why are leaves left lying in the garden good for hedgehogs?
9678.e: Under piles of leaves, hedgehogs find insects to eat and a good place to hide. That is why you should not clear away all the leaves in autumn.
9678.m: Leaf piles give hedgehogs shelter and food.

9679.q: What is the minimum age to be elected to the National Council?
9679.e: In Switzerland, anyone who is allowed to vote may also stand for election to the National Council. So the minimum age is 18.
9679.m: From 18 you can stand as a candidate.

9680.q: What is the kingfisher’s short, strong tail for?
a: it helps it steer during fast flying manoeuvres
it is used for climbing trees
it is fanned out like a wheel when courting
it protects against predators like a spine
9680.e: The short, firm tail helps the kingfisher steer during fast flight and tight turns. Without it, it would be less agile.
9680.m: A short tail steers fast flying manoeuvres.

9681.q: The red kite’s scientific name is “Milvus milvus”. What is striking about this name?
9681.e: Every animal species has a scientific name made of two words. For the red kite, both words are the same: Milvus milvus.
9681.m: The red kite’s scientific name is Milvus milvus.

9682.q: Roughly how heavy is an edible dormouse outside its hibernation period?
9682.e: A normal edible dormouse usually weighs between 120 and 180 grams. Before hibernation this weight can rise considerably.
9682.m: The weight is usually 120 to 180 grams.

9683.q: Roughly how big is an adult grey heron from head to tail?
9683.e: With a body length of almost a metre, the grey heron is one of the largest birds in our part of the world. On top of that, its long neck makes it look even bigger.
9683.m: Grey herons are almost a metre long.

9684.q: How do newborn red deer calves hide from danger?
a: They lie still and hidden in tall grass
They follow the whole herd at once
9684.e: Newborn calves lie still and hidden for the first few days. Their spotted coat helps them avoid being discovered.
9684.m: Calves hide quietly in the grass.

9685.q: What is the basic legal status of the wolf in Switzerland?
a: It may be hunted all year without rules
It is officially classed as a pet
It is treated like a pest
9685.e: The wolf is basically protected in Switzerland because it once almost died out. Under certain conditions, however, the law can allow its numbers to be controlled.
9685.m: The wolf is basically a protected species.

9686.q: What does a large, bright red comb on a cockerel usually show?
9686.e: A strong red comb is often a sign that a cockerel is healthy and has good blood flow. A pale comb can point to illness.
9686.m: A red comb shows good health.

9687.q: How does the Roman snail seal its shell in winter?
a: With a chalky lid made from slime
9687.e: In winter the snail forms a thin chalky lid called the epiphragm. It closes the opening of the shell.
9687.m: A chalky lid protects it in winter.

9688.q: What is the building where chickens live called?
9688.e: The henhouse protects the chickens from the weather and enemies. They also sleep there at night.

9689.q: What is the highland where many alpacas live called?
9689.e: The Altiplano is a high plateau in the Andes. There the air is thin and the nights are cold.
9689.m: The Altiplano is the highland of the Andes.

9690.q: What is the legal status of the stoat in Switzerland?
a: It may be hunted at any time
It may be kept like a hamster
9690.e: In Switzerland the stoat is a protected wild animal. So it must not simply be hunted or caught.
9690.m: The stoat is protected in Switzerland.

9691.q: From which animal is the domestic pig originally descended?
9691.e: Thousands of years ago, people tamed wild boar. Over many generations, today’s domestic pig developed from them.
9691.m: The domestic pig is descended from the wild boar.

9692.q: What do you get when a cloud reaches right down to the ground?
9692.e: Fog is made of tiny water droplets floating in the air. It is really a cloud lying on the ground.
9692.m: Fog is a cloud on the ground.

9693.q: How can you often recognise a grey heron in flight from far away?
a: By slow, deep wingbeats and a tucked-in neck
By fast, fluttering wingbeats like a hummingbird
By its neck stretched out straight
9693.e: The grey heron’s flight is marked by slow and deep wingbeats. Together with the tucked-in neck, its shape in flight is very typical.
9693.m: Slow wingbeats give the grey heron away.

9694.q: What are the okapi’s broad back teeth made for?
9694.e: The okapi is a plant eater. With its broad back teeth it grinds leaves and shoots.
9694.m: Okapi teeth are made for plants.

9695.q: How does the adder catch its prey?
a: It bites and waits for the venom to work
9695.e: The bitten animal often still runs off a little way. The snake follows the scent trail and finds it.
9695.m: First bite, then follow the trail.

9696.q: How is a pond skater’s body divided into parts?
9696.e: This is true of all insects. The six legs are attached to the thorax.
9696.m: An insect’s body has a head, thorax and abdomen.

9698.q: Roughly how much can an adult common raven weigh?
9698.e: Weighing around one kilogram, the common raven is one of the heaviest songbirds of all. Its strong build supports this weight.

9699.q: Why does an earthworm also swallow tiny stones when it eats?
a: They help grind up the food in its stomach
It builds its tunnels with them
It collects them as a store
9699.e: Tiny stones get into the stomach together with the soil. There they help grind up the food as in a mill.

9700.q: What does a budgie cage absolutely need?
a: Enough space to fly and several perches
Just a small box with no perches
9700.e: Budgies need lots of space to fly and move about. Different perches help them stay active.

10277.q: On which continent does the serval live in the wild?
10277.e: The serval is widespread across large parts of Africa south of the Sahara, with small remaining populations in the north of the continent.
10277.m: The serval is a purely African wild cat.

12474.q: How many eyes does a tarantula have?
12474.e: Tarantulas have eight small eyes, usually arranged in two rows on a little mound. They see poorly and rely mainly on touch and vibrations.
12474.m: Despite eight eyes, a tarantula sees poorly.

12870.q: What did the Earth form from?
12870.e: Dust and lumps of rock were circling in space. They crashed into each other and stuck together into bigger and bigger lumps until the Earth was formed.
12870.m: The Earth formed from dust and rock circling in space.

12871.e: The Sun formed first. Then the planets, including the Earth, formed from what was left around the Sun.
12871.m: The Sun is older than the Earth.

12872.q: What was the Earth like at the very beginning?
12872.e: The young Earth was so hot that its rock glowed and was liquid. Only slowly did it cool down.
12872.m: The young Earth was glowing hot.

12873.e: Lava is rock that is so hot it becomes liquid. It comes out of the Earth at volcanoes.
12873.m: Lava is liquid, glowing hot rock.

12874.q: According to scientists today, how was the Moon formed?
12874.e: Scientists think that a large body in space crashed into the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris.
12874.m: The Moon probably formed after a big collision with the Earth.

12875.q: Where did the first life on Earth appear?
12875.e: Scientists think that the first living things appeared in water. The water probably protected them from the Sun’s dangerous rays.
12875.m: The first life probably appeared in water.

12876.q: How big were the first living things?
12876.e: The first living things were so small that you can only see them with a microscope. They were single-celled organisms like bacteria.
12876.m: The first living things were tiny single-celled organisms.

12877.q: Which planet is the Earth, counting from the Sun?
12877.e: From the Sun, first come Mercury and Venus, then the Earth. That is why the Earth is the third planet.
12877.m: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.

12878.e: The Earth is almost as round as a ball. You can see this clearly on photos taken from space.
12878.m: The Earth is almost the shape of a ball.

12879.q: What was there a lot of on the young Earth?
12879.e: On the young Earth volcanoes erupted everywhere. There were no plants or animals yet.
12879.m: There were very many volcanoes on the young Earth.

12880.q: What formed when the Earth slowly cooled down and it rained for a long time?
12880.e: When the Earth cooled down, water vapour turned into rain. The water collected in the low places and formed the seas.
12880.m: When the Earth cooled down, the seas formed.

12881.q: What is it like deep inside the Earth?
12881.e: Inside the Earth it is still very hot today. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets.
12881.m: Inside the Earth it is very hot.

12882.q: What is the centre of the Earth called?
12882.e: Right in the middle of the Earth is the core. It is made mainly of iron.
12882.m: The centre of the Earth is called the core.

12883.q: What is the outermost, solid layer of the Earth that we live on called?
12883.e: The Earth’s crust is the outer, solid layer of the Earth. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin of an apple.
12883.m: We live on the Earth’s crust.

12884.q: Who lived on Earth first: fish or dinosaurs?
12884.e: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs. The dinosaurs came much later.
12884.m: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs.

12885.q: Do the continents always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, they are tied to the seabed.
12885.e: The continents move only a few centimetres each year. But over millions of years they travel a long way.
12885.m: The continents move very slowly across the Earth.

12886.q: What was the name of the huge continent at the time of the first dinosaurs, in which almost all land was joined together?
12886.e: More than 200 million years ago, when the first dinosaurs lived, almost all the land on Earth was joined together. This giant continent is called Pangaea.
12886.m: The giant continent Pangaea later broke up into today’s continents.

12887.e: Africa slowly pushed against Europe. The rock was squeezed together and folded upwards, and that is how the Alps were formed.
12887.m: The Alps were formed because rock was pushed together.

12888.q: What do people sometimes find high up in the Swiss Alps?
12888.e: The rock of the Alps used to lie on the seabed. That is why fossilised shells and snails are found up there.
12888.m: Fossilised sea creatures are found in the Alps.

12889.e: The word comes from Greek. “Deinos” means terrible and “sauros” means lizard.

a: They were born alive like calves.
They grew in their mother’s pouch.
12890.e: Dinosaurs laid eggs, just as birds and crocodiles do today. Scientists have found many fossilised dinosaur eggs.

12891.e: Tyrannosaurus rex was a big meat-eater. It had a huge mouth with sharp teeth.

12892.q: What was strikingly small on Tyrannosaurus rex?
12892.e: Tyrannosaurus rex had a huge head and strong legs. But its arms were very short.
12892.m: Tyrannosaurus rex had very short arms.

12893.q: On how many legs did Tyrannosaurus rex walk?
12893.e: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on its two powerful back legs. It kept its balance with its long tail.
12893.m: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on two legs.

12894.q: How many horns did Triceratops have on its face?
12894.e: “Triceratops” means three-horned face. It had two long horns above its eyes and a short one on its nose.
12894.m: Triceratops had three horns on its face.

12895.e: Triceratops was a plant-eater. It used its beak to pluck plants.

12896.q: What was especially long on Brachiosaurus?
12896.e: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck. This let it eat leaves high up in the trees.
12896.m: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck.

12897.q: What did Stegosaurus have on its back?
12897.e: Stegosaurus had a row of large bony plates on its back. On its tail it had sharp spikes.
12897.m: Stegosaurus had large plates on its back.

12898.q: What did Ankylosaurus have at the end of its tail?
12898.e: Ankylosaurus had armour made of bony plates. At the end of its tail it had a heavy club of bone that it could use to defend itself.
12898.m: Ankylosaurus had a bony club on its tail.

12899.q: What did some dinosaurs, for example Velociraptor, have?
12899.e: Scientists have found out that many smaller dinosaurs had feathers. Velociraptor was one of them.

12900.q: Which animals today are descended from dinosaurs?
12900.e: Birds developed from small, feathered dinosaurs. You could say that birds are today’s dinosaurs.

12901.q: What do we call scientists who study dinosaur fossils?
12901.e: Palaeontologists study living things from prehistoric times. They dig up fossils and examine them.

12902.q: How do we know what dinosaurs looked like?
12902.e: Nobody has ever seen a dinosaur. Scientists put fossilised bones together and so find out how the animals were built.
12902.m: Fossilised bones show us what dinosaurs looked like.

12903.q: Did humans and dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus rex live at the same time?
12903.e: Many millions of years lie between the big dinosaurs and the first humans. Films in which people fight dinosaurs are made up.
12903.m: Humans and big dinosaurs never lived at the same time.

12904.q: Which period of Earth’s history is named after the Jura mountains?
12904.e: The Jurassic is a period when many dinosaurs lived. It is named after the Jura mountains, where rock from this time was studied.
12904.m: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura mountains.

12905.q: Which dinosaur has often been found in Frick in the canton of Aargau?
12905.e: Many Plateosaurus skeletons were found in a clay pit in Frick. You can see them in the dinosaur museum in Frick.
12905.m: Many Plateosaurus were found in Frick in Aargau.

12906.q: What can you see near Lommiswil in the canton of Solothurn?
12906.e: In an old quarry near Lommiswil you can see many dinosaur footprints on a large slab of rock. They are about 145 million years old.
12906.m: There are dinosaur footprints near Lommiswil.

a: No, some were as small as a chicken.
Yes, all were bigger than a house.
Yes, all were bigger than an elephant.
No, all were as tiny as ants.
12907.e: There were huge dinosaurs, but small ones too. Some were only as big as a chicken.

12908.q: Roughly how many years ago did the dinosaurs die out?
12908.e: That is so long ago that it is hard to imagine. At that time the age of the big dinosaurs came to an end.
12908.m: The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

12909.q: What hit the Earth shortly before the dinosaurs died out?
12909.e: A huge asteroid crashed into the Earth. That was the main reason the dinosaurs died out.
12909.m: A huge asteroid hit the Earth.

a: A lump of rock in space
A small moon of the Earth
12910.e: Asteroids are lumps of rock or metal that circle the Sun. Some are small, others are many kilometres across.
12910.m: An asteroid is a lump of rock in space.

12911.q: Roughly how big was the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs?
a: About as big as a car
About as big as a football
12911.e: The asteroid was about 10 to 15 kilometres across. That is more than the height of the highest mountain on Earth.
12911.m: The asteroid was many kilometres across.

12912.q: In which present-day country is the asteroid’s crater?
12912.e: The crater is on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. It is called the Chicxulub crater and is covered over today.
12912.m: The asteroid’s crater is in Mexico.

12913.q: What happened to the sky after the impact?
a: There were never any clouds again.
12913.e: The impact threw huge amounts of dust and soot into the air. They darkened the sky for a long time.
12913.m: After the impact, dust darkened the sky.

12914.q: Why did it become cold on Earth after the impact?
a: Sunlight could no longer get through.
12914.e: The dust in the air blocked the sunlight. That is why it became dark and cold all over the Earth for a long time.
12914.m: Without sunlight it became cold on Earth.

12915.q: Roughly how many kinds of animals and plants died out at that time?
a: About three out of four kinds
About one out of a hundred kinds
12915.e: Scientists estimate that about three quarters of all kinds of animals and plants died out at that time. It was one of the biggest mass extinctions in Earth’s history.
12915.m: About three out of four kinds died out at that time.

12916.q: Why did the big plant-eaters also have problems afterwards?
12916.e: Because many plants died, the big plant-eaters could no longer find enough to eat. After that the meat-eaters had no prey either.
12916.m: Without plants the plant-eaters had no food.

12917.q: Apart from the asteroid, what probably also had an effect?
a: Huge forest fires started by people
12917.e: At about the same time huge volcanoes erupted in India. They also changed the climate on Earth.
12917.m: Huge volcanic eruptions also made life hard for the animals.

12918.q: Which animals survived when the dinosaurs died out?
12918.e: Small mammals needed little food and could hide. So many of them survived.
12918.m: Small mammals survived the extinction of the dinosaurs.

12919.q: Which group of animals survived the extinction and still lives today?
12919.e: Crocodiles already existed at the time of the dinosaurs. Some smaller crocodiles survived the great extinction.
12919.m: Crocodiles survived the extinction of the dinosaurs.

12920.q: Which plants were the first to spread again in many places after the impact?
12920.e: Ferns were able to spread again quickly after the disaster. In some places scientists find especially many fern spores in rock layers from this time.
12920.m: After the impact, ferns were the first to spread.

12921.q: With which period of Earth’s history did the age of the big dinosaurs end?
12921.e: The last big dinosaurs lived in the Cretaceous period. At the end of the Cretaceous they died out, long before there were humans.
12921.m: The age of the big dinosaurs ended with the Cretaceous.

12922.q: Which sea creatures with coiled shells died out together with the dinosaurs?
12922.e: Ammonites were sea creatures with a coiled shell, related to squid. They died out in the same great extinction as the dinosaurs.
12922.m: Ammonites died out together with the dinosaurs.

12923.q: Did the dinosaurs die out in a single day?
12923.e: Many animals died right at the impact. Others only died later, because the cold and hunger lasted a long time.
12923.m: The dinosaurs took longer than one day to die out.

12924.q: What formed when the asteroid struck a sea?
12924.e: The asteroid crashed into a shallow sea. This created huge flood waves that rushed far over the coasts.
12924.m: The impact set off huge flood waves.

12925.q: Which big meat-eater was one of the last dinosaurs?
12925.e: Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs. It died out in the great extinction.
12925.m: Tyrannosaurus rex was one of the last dinosaurs.

12926.q: How do scientists know that an asteroid struck at that time?
a: From stories told by early humans
12926.e: Scientists have found a thin layer of rock from that time all over the world. It contains substances that come from space.
12926.m: Traces in the rock reveal the asteroid impact.

12927.q: Kinds of animals are dying out today too. Who is often to blame for this today?
12927.e: Today kinds of animals often die out because people destroy their habitats or hunt them too much. That is why protecting nature is important.
12927.m: Today kinds of animals often die out because of people.

12928.q: On which continent did the first humans live?
12928.e: The first humans lived in Africa. From there they later spread all over the world.
12928.m: The first humans lived in Africa.

12929.q: What could early humans do better than apes?
12929.e: Early humans walked upright on two legs. This left their hands free for tools.
12929.m: Early humans walked upright on two legs.

12930.q: What is the name of the famous skeleton of an early human female from Ethiopia?
12930.e: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in Africa. She lived more than 3 million years ago and already walked upright.
12930.m: Lucy is a famous skeleton from Africa.

12931.q: What did the first humans make their tools from?
12931.e: The first humans shaped stones so that they had sharp edges. They did not yet know about metal and glass.
12931.m: The first tools were made of stone.

12932.q: Why is the Stone Age called that?
a: Because tools were made of stone
Because all houses were made of stone
12932.e: In the Stone Age people made many tools and weapons from stone. They did not yet know about metal.
12932.m: The Stone Age is called that because the tools were made of stone.

12933.q: What is the name of a large stone tool that was held in one hand?
12933.e: The hand axe was a stone that was chipped sharp on both sides. It fitted well in the hand.
12933.m: The hand axe was an important Stone Age tool.

12934.q: Which stone was especially popular for sharp tools in the Stone Age?
12934.e: Flint is easy to split and gets very sharp edges. It is also called silex.
12934.m: Flint was especially popular for sharp tools.

12935.q: What gave early humans warmth and light at night?
12935.e: Early humans learned to use fire. It gave warmth and light, kept wild animals away and made food softer.
12935.m: Fire gave early humans warmth and light.

12936.q: How did the first humans get their food?
12936.e: The first humans were hunter-gatherers. They hunted animals and gathered berries, nuts, roots and mushrooms. Fields and farm animals only came much later.

12937.q: Where did early humans often live?
12937.e: Many early humans lived in caves or under rock overhangs. They also built tents from wood and animal skins.
12937.m: Early humans often lived in caves and tents.

12938.q: Why did early humans often move on?
a: They followed the animals and the food.
12938.e: Hunter-gatherers followed the herds of animals and looked for new plants. That is why they rarely stayed in the same place for long.

12939.q: What did Stone Age people make their clothes from?
12939.e: Stone Age people sewed their clothes from furs and leather. This kept them warm in winter.
12939.m: In the Stone Age people wore clothes made of fur.

12940.q: What did Stone Age people sew with?
12940.e: Stone Age people carved fine needles from bone. They did not yet know about metal.
12940.m: Stone Age people sewed with bone needles.

12941.q: What did Stone Age people paint on cave walls?
12941.e: Many cave paintings show animals such as horses, bison and deer. The pictures are many thousands of years old.
12941.m: Stone Age people painted animals on cave walls.

12942.q: In which country is the famous painted cave of Lascaux?
12942.e: The cave of Lascaux is in France. Its animal pictures are many thousands of years old.
12942.m: The painted cave of Lascaux is in France.

12943.q: Which animal was probably the first pet of humans?
12943.e: The dog is descended from the wolf. According to what we know today, it was the first animal to live together with people. One of the oldest dog finds comes from the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen.
12943.m: The dog was probably the first pet of humans.

12944.q: What are the early humans called who lived in Europe before us?
12944.e: The Neanderthals lived in Europe for a long time, including during the Ice Age. They are named after the Neander Valley in Germany.
12944.m: The Neanderthals lived in Europe before us.

12945.q: What is the name of the human species that all people today belong to?
12945.e: All people today belong to the species Homo sapiens. This is Latin and means “wise human”.
12945.m: All people today belong to Homo sapiens.

12946.q: Which musical instrument did Stone Age people already make?
12946.e: Scientists have found flutes made of bird bones and mammoth ivory. The oldest are more than 40,000 years old.
12946.m: There were bone flutes even in the Stone Age.

12947.q: What did Stone Age people often hunt with?
12947.e: Stone Age hunters used spears with tips made of stone or bone. They often hunted together.
12947.m: Stone Age hunters hunted with spears.

12948.q: What was it like in the Ice Age?
12948.e: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today. Large parts of the Earth were covered with ice.
12948.m: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today.

12949.q: What covered large parts of Switzerland in the Ice Age?
12949.e: In the Ice Age the glaciers from the Alps grew far out into the Swiss Plateau. At the coldest times most of Switzerland lay under ice.
12949.m: In the Ice Age a large part of Switzerland lay under glaciers.

12950.q: Which animal with long fur and tusks lived in the Ice Age?
12950.e: The mammoth had long, curved tusks. Thick, long fur protected it from the cold.
12950.m: The mammoth had thick fur against the cold.

12951.q: Which animal today is the mammoth related to?
12951.e: The mammoth belongs to the elephant family. Like elephants, it had a trunk and tusks.
12951.m: The mammoth is related to the elephant.

12952.q: In which village in the canton of Zurich were many mammoth bones found?
12952.e: Bones of several mammoths were found in Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich. You can see the finds in the Mammoth Museum.
12952.m: Many mammoth bones were found in Niederweningen.

12953.q: Which rhinoceros lived in Europe in the Ice Age?
12953.e: The woolly rhinoceros had thick, shaggy fur. This let it live in the cold of the Ice Age.
12953.m: The woolly rhinoceros lived in Europe in the Ice Age.

12954.q: Which big bear from the Ice Age is extinct today?
12954.e: The cave bear was bigger than today’s brown bear and spent the winter resting in caves. Its bones have also been found in Swiss caves such as the Wildkirchli in the Alpstein.
12954.m: The cave bear lived in the Ice Age and is extinct today.

12955.q: Which cat with very long canine teeth lived in the Ice Age?
12955.e: The sabre-toothed cat had two very long upper canine teeth. It is extinct today.
12955.m: The sabre-toothed cat had very long canine teeth.

12956.q: Which animals that live in the far north today also lived in Switzerland in the Ice Age?
12956.e: In the cold Ice Age reindeer also lived in Switzerland. Today they live only in the far north.
12956.m: There were reindeer in Switzerland in the Ice Age.

a: A big stone carried along by a glacier
An animal frozen in the ice
A bird from the Ice Age
12957.e: Glaciers carried huge stones far away from their mountains. When the ice melted, they were left behind. They are called erratic boulders.
12957.m: An erratic boulder is a stone brought by a glacier.

12958.q: What helped to shape many Swiss lakes, for example Lake Zurich?
12958.e: The Ice Age glaciers carved out deep valleys. When the ice melted, they filled with water and became lakes.
12958.m: Many Swiss lakes were shaped by glaciers.

12960.q: Roughly how many years ago did the last ice age end?
12960.e: The last ice age came to an end about 12,000 years ago. After that it became warmer and the glaciers melted.
12960.m: The last ice age ended about 12,000 years ago.

12961.q: What happened when the Ice Age came to an end?
12961.e: At the end of the Ice Age it became warmer. The glaciers melted and retreated into the Alps.
12961.m: At the end of the Ice Age the glaciers melted.

12962.q: What was the sea level like in the Ice Age?
12962.e: In the Ice Age a lot of water was frozen in glaciers. That is why the sea level was lower than today.
12962.m: In the Ice Age the sea level was lower than today.

12963.q: Were there already people in the Ice Age?
a: Yes, they hunted wild horses, for example.
12963.e: People lived long before the end of the Ice Age. They hunted wild horses and bison, for example.
12963.m: There were already people in the Ice Age.

12964.q: What is the name of the largest glacier in the Alps?
12964.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the largest and longest glacier in the Alps. But in the Ice Age the glaciers were much bigger still.
12964.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.

12965.q: Which large animal did people in the Ice Age sometimes hunt together?
12965.e: A mammoth was too big for a single hunter. That is why people sometimes hunted it in groups.
12965.m: In the Ice Age, people sometimes hunted mammoths.

12966.q: What did Ice Age people use from a mammoth?
12966.e: People used almost everything from a mammoth: meat for eating, fur for clothes and bones for tools.
12966.m: People used the meat, fur and bones of the mammoth.

12967.q: Which tool did not exist yet in the Stone Age?
12967.e: People in the Stone Age did not yet know about iron. Tools were made of stone, wood and bone.
12967.m: There were no iron tools in the Stone Age.

12968.q: Which age followed the Stone Age in Europe?
12968.e: After the Stone Age, people learned how to make bronze. That is why the next great age is called the Bronze Age.
12968.m: The Bronze Age followed the Stone Age.

12969.q: What is the oldest part of the Stone Age called?
12969.e: The Old Stone Age is the oldest and longest part of the Stone Age. It lasted much longer than all the later parts put together.
12969.m: The Old Stone Age is the oldest part of the Stone Age.

12970.q: What is the last part of the Stone Age called?
12970.e: The New Stone Age is the most recent part of the Stone Age. After it came the age of metals.
12970.m: The New Stone Age is the last part of the Stone Age.

12971.q: Roughly how long did the Stone Age last?
12971.e: The oldest stone tools are more than two million years old. This makes the Stone Age the longest period in human history.
12971.m: The Stone Age is the longest period in human history.

12972.q: What did NOT exist yet in the Stone Age?
12972.e: Stone Age people in Europe could not write yet. That is why much of what we know about them comes only from finds in the ground.
12972.m: Stone Age people could not write yet.

12973.q: Who searches the ground for traces from the Stone Age?
12973.e: Archaeologists dig carefully in the ground. They find tools, bones and the remains of houses.
12973.m: Archaeologists find traces of the Stone Age in the ground.

12974.q: What is the name of the famous glacier mummy found in the Alps?
12974.e: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the ice of the Ötztal Alps. He lived around 5300 years ago, at the end of the Stone Age.
12974.m: Ötzi is a man from the Stone Age who was found in the ice.

12975.q: What was it like in the Ice Age, when many Stone Age people lived?
12975.e: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today. Huge glaciers also covered large parts of Switzerland.
12975.m: In the Ice Age, most of Switzerland was covered in ice.

12976.q: What did people gather in the Stone Age?
12976.e: People gathered berries, nuts, mushrooms, roots and herbs. This was an important part of their food.
12976.m: Hunter-gatherers also ate berries, nuts and mushrooms.

12978.q: What do we call people who do not live in one fixed place?
12978.e: Nomads move from place to place. Hunter-gatherers lived like this.
12978.m: Nomads do not always live in the same place.

12980.q: What did hunters use from an animal they had killed?
12980.e: They ate the meat and made clothes from the fur. They made tools from bones and antlers.
12980.m: Hunters used almost everything from an animal.

12981.q: Which animal did people often hunt in the Ice Age?
12981.e: In the Ice Age, large herds of reindeer lived in our region. They were very important for hunters.
12981.m: In the Ice Age, people often hunted reindeer.

12982.e: Hunter-gatherers lived in small groups, often with their family. Together they could hunt better and protect themselves.

12984.q: Why did people in the Stone Age use caves?
a: As a hiding place for gold
12984.e: Caves gave shelter from cold, rain and wind. People often lived at the entrance of the cave.
12984.m: Caves gave people shelter from the weather and the cold.

12985.q: Where else did Stone Age people often live when there was no cave?
12985.e: Many Stone Age people lived in tents made of animal skins and poles. Not everyone lived in caves.
12985.m: Many Stone Age people lived in tents made of skins.

12988.q: Which early humans are named after a valley in Germany?
12988.e: The Neanderthals are named after the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf. Their bones were found there.
12988.m: The Neanderthals are named after a valley in Germany.

12989.q: Which large Ice Age animal hibernated in caves?
12989.e: The cave bear was much bigger than a brown bear today and ate mainly plants. In winter it slept in caves, where many of its bones have been found.
12989.m: The cave bear spent the winter in caves.

12990.q: Where did Stone Age people sleep?
12990.e: People put furs, grass or leaves on the ground. They slept on them, often close to the fire.
12990.m: Stone Age people slept on furs on the ground.

12991.q: What did Stone Age people like to wear as jewellery?
12991.e: People made necklaces from shells, animal teeth and stones. They did not know about metal or glass yet.
12991.m: Jewellery made of shells and animal teeth existed even in the Stone Age.

12992.q: Which famous cave in Switzerland is near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen?
12992.e: In the Kesslerloch near Thayngen, many tools, pieces of jewellery and animal bones from the Ice Age were found. It is one of the most important sites in Switzerland.
12992.m: The Kesslerloch near Thayngen is a famous Ice Age site.

12993.q: Which animal is shown in the famous engraving from the Kesslerloch?
12993.e: In the Kesslerloch, a piece of reindeer antler with an engraved reindeer was found. Today it is called the “Searching Reindeer”; it used to be called the “Grazing Reindeer”.
12993.m: An engraved reindeer was found in the Kesslerloch.

12994.q: What did Stone Age people need fire for?
12994.e: Fire gave warmth and light. People could also roast meat with it.
12994.m: Fire gave people warmth, light and cooked food.

12995.q: Which animals did fire keep away?
12995.e: Many wild animals are afraid of fire. So people were better protected at night.
12995.m: Fire protected people from wild animals.

12996.q: How could Stone Age people make fire?
12996.e: People struck a flint against a stone such as pyrite. The sparks fell onto dry material.
12996.m: You could strike sparks for a fire with stones.

12997.q: How can you make fire without stones?
12997.e: If you spin a wooden stick quickly on a board, the wood gets hot. This makes a small glowing ember.
12997.m: Rubbing wood quickly can make an ember.

12998.q: What is the dry material that catches the sparks first called?
12998.e: Tinder catches sparks easily and starts to glow. People used, for example, a dried tree fungus.
12998.m: Tinder catches sparks and starts to glow.

12999.q: Where did the first humans probably get their first fire from?
12999.e: Lightning could set a tree on fire. The first humans took fire from such fires and looked after it carefully.
12999.m: The first humans probably took fire from fires caused by lightning.

13000.q: What was placed around a fireplace?
13000.e: Stones around the fire kept it together. Archaeologists often recognise old fireplaces by such stones and ash.
13000.m: Fireplaces were often ringed with stones.

13001.q: What is left in the ground from an old fire?
13001.e: Burnt wood turns into charcoal and ash. This shows archaeologists where a fire once burned.
13001.m: Charcoal and ash show where a fire burned.

13002.e: Cooked or roasted meat is softer. It is easier to chew and to digest.
13002.m: Roasted meat is softer and easier to eat.

13003.q: Which stone was especially popular for tools?
13003.e: Flint breaks into sharp pieces. It was good for cutting and scraping.

13004.q: What is a large stone tool that you hold in your fist called?
